speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the right hon. the Prime Minister in connection with the visit to Canada of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. subsubtopic: MIDDLE AND FAR EAST-PROPOSED WITHDRAWAL OF BRITISH FORCES

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address this question to the right hon. Prime Minister. In view of the disastrous escalation on both sides of the war in Viet Nam and in view of some very frank suggestions made by Senator Robert Kennedy only yesterday, could the Prime Minister inform the house whether there has been any encouraging or other word from Canada's envoy at Hanoi who I understand has been there for three weeks.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REPORT BY CANADIAN REPRESENTATIVE AT HANOI
speechtext:
Yes. He has been there longer than he expected. As my hon. friend may have learned, at least from the newspapers, it has been difficult to get a plane from Saigon to Hanoi to bring him back, in the present deplorable situation in that capital. We have not heard from him in recent days, and I should prefer not to make any comment on his mission or what might come from that mission until we receive a report from him.

I should be happy to make a short statement on this bill. For a great number of years there has been a feeling in that particular area north of the sixtieth parallel that certain services for which the government and this parliament are responsible are not available with that degree of efficiency that is expected in other parts of Canada.
When I assumed my responsibilities here the first thing I heard in that vast territory was that they wanted what they called government on the ground. One of the most distressing aspects of administration that I heard
Procedure for Granting Territorial Lands about was the difficulty of acquiring the right to crown lands in the two territories. The procedure that had been adopted over the years was resulting in delays of up to, I was told, five, six, and even eight months. At that time, of course, the registration of these lands was by letters patent, and the proposal now is to replace that by a simple fiat from myself, as minister, to the appropriate registrar of land titles.
We expect to have the registrar of land titles located very definitely on the ground, and it is our hope that we can give the people living in those territories the opportunity of acquiring those lands in a matter of as little as a week or ten days, if everything is in order.
This bill, Your Honour, came to us from the other place, where it was passed. It is a housekeeping bill and is designed to give the type of efficient service to those who live north of the sixtieth parallel, in respect of acquiring crown lands, that they might expect to receive in other parts of Canada. If the Fathers of Confederation had not had the vision to anticipate what would come out of the great movement from the colonial status of the Northwest Territories they would have used exactly the same arguments as are being used today, namely, that the population base and economic resources were not substantial enough. Indeed when it was decided to build a railway into the northwest it was described by a Liberal opposition as a railway that would go from wigwam to wigwam and would not pay for its own axle grease. Much the same arguments are being used by a Liberal government now in opposing progress toward self-government in the territories.
We all realize that progress toward selfgovernment will be gradual. We are not going to have provincial governments overnight. There has to be a series of gradual movements toward this goal. This legislation could have provided a golden opportunity to move forward in the area of resource control. At this stage no one is asking that the legislative council of the Yukon have control over such resources as oil, minerals, water and so forth. But so far as surface land resources are concerned that control could have been given in toto to the Yukon government. It would have given a tremendous boost to the morale of those Yukoners who are away ahead of us in parliament and ahead of the government in demanding that they be masters of their own fate and captains of their own destiny in the field of democratic government.
We all agree that rapid progress has been made. What we now need to be convinced of is that if this forward momentum is to continue the next step is self-government so that the people themselves will be strongly motivated to carry out the responsibilities that should rightfully be theirs in the area of public administration. Procrastination is the thief of time. Studies are good. The Carrothers report has merely verified what northerners have known for years. The white paper which is to be tabled in the Yukon will merely be a rehash of many of the things put forward in the recent resolution of the Yukon council, which was partially placed on the record by the hon. member for Yukon. It is not studies and white papers that are needed now. It is action on the part of the government.

Mr. Chairman, as one who held brief responsibility for the administration of the Territorial Lands Act I should like to make one or two remarks on this bill. I hope they will be helpful not only to the minister and the commissioners of the two territories but to the people in these areas. One of the responsibilities that bears most heavily on the minister, who has had the responsibility of initiating the transfer of crown lands into the hands of private individuals, is the protection of future generations in these territories and acting as trustee for them. In my experience, the amount of time I put in trying to make certain that there was no abuse of the right of future generations to access to the land of the territories was considerable. Yet I do not begrudge that time for the simple reason that until we have evolved a system of responsible government in the territories, under which these duties can be carried out with complete

Procedure for Granting Territorial Lands responsibility to the electors, this responsibility remains and does bear heavily on a minister.
The technique of speeding up the transfer of crown lands to the individual has been improved under this bill. I do not think there is any question about that. The problem that concerns me as a matter of conscience is the fact that there are in the territories two groups of people who have not the same protections that people have in the provinces. I am speaking about the Indians particularly and I suppose eventually the Eskimos. If my memory serves me correctly, there are no treaties which cover the Indians in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, or at least they were never promulgated. Therefore even on reservations the Indians do not have protection in these areas.
I have talked with the Indians in these areas. They still follow the traditional, cultural habit of moving into an area because the factor of transportation is their main concern and they squat, if you will, along a river, around a lake or some place where it is convenient to get from one area to another. Over a period of time they sometimes change the places in which they squat and settle in a village.
I recall a personal approach that I made to one group of Indians in regard to giving them title to their land in a particular area in order that they would be protected from any person coming in, asking for and getting a grant of land over which the Indians had prior squatters' rights. This is a matter you cannot deal with specifically in this legislation. The responsibility is a subjective one which falls on the minister or the commissioners, as clause 3 of the bill points out.
I ask the minister not only to consider this problem but to advise the commissioners that the persons who have the responsibility for signing the notifications should consider the problem of the Indians and see that in no case does the requirement for private property take over an area in which the squatters' rights of the Indians are paramount. Squatters' rights are an ancient part of the customs in undeveloped areas. I want to make certain that the minister will ensure that in no case will the officers of the commissioner or the minister's officers allow anybody to move into any area in which an interest is held by the Indians if that move is not legal. I do not know how this can be done legally but it is a matter which falls under the jurisdiction of the commissioner or the minister.

The second point I wish to make is that I agree with those who have said that there is a strong desire on the part of the people in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories to acquire more responsibility. I strongly believe that regardless of the financial inability of the territories to govern themselves completely at this time, we must carry on the precedent we set by granting them the financial status which we have given them in the agreements and by encouraging them at every step to take on more responsibility. speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING LETTING OF CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it would be helpful if I were to make a short statement. I should begin by pointing out that this is a bill which has been considered at some length and approved by the Senate. It is a simple bill of a housekeeping and unexciting nature. The purpose is to achieve a more efficient way of doing government business than is possible under the present act. This bill arises from the recommendations made by the Glassco commission. Members of the house will recall that the royal commission under Mr. Glassco discovered that the paperwork involved in the letting of government contracts was unnecessarily detailed and recommended that there be a substantial further delegation of the authority to enter into contracts.
The result of this was that in respect of government contracts, not otherwise governed by statute, and entered into under authority of the government's contract regulations, the Treasury Board would delegate the authority for entering into contracts to departments on a much larger scale than had been the case hitherto. However, contracts entered into by the Department of Defence Production on behalf of the Department of National Defence are entered into under the authority of the Defence Production Act. The Defence Production Act as presently written in section 17, subsection (1), paragraphs (d) and (e), provides a limitation on the authority of the minister to enter into contracts without government approval of the governor in council in
Defence Production Act the amount of $25,000 in cases where no tenders are called, or where there is only one tenderer, and in the amount of $50,000 where there is more than one tender and where the contract is awarded to the lowest tenderer.
Under the government contract regulations evolved as a consequence of the recommendation of the Glassco commission, the authority of departments to enter into contracts without the further authority of the Treasury Board, but with a provision for reporting on such contracts entered into, is limited to contracts in the amount of $250,000 where there have been no tenders or where there is only one tenderer, and $500,000 where there is more than one tender and where the lowest tender has been accepted and a contract has resulted therefrom. There is an obligation periodically to report such contracts to the Treasury Board. The result of this has been that the Department of Defence Production, which has been progressively taking over the purchasing responsibilities of civil departments, and will be taking over the procurement work for all government departments, both civil and military, finds that where procurement is undertaken on behalf of civil departments the arrangements for contracting are carried out within the limitation laid down by the Treasury Board now, namely $250,000 and $500,000.
Where contracts are entered into for the Department of National Defence in respect of defence contracts there is a limitation of $25,000 and $50,000 which involves as a consequence not only disparate procedures but a vast amount of what I think the Glassco commission recognizes to be unnecessary paperwork. The purpose of this amendment is to alter the Defence Production Act in such a way that the procurement for defence purposes under this act will be subject to the same rules and regulations as procurement for civil departments, through the delegated authority from the Treasury Board.
I should point out that in addition to making the limits correspond this also removes a provision in the present act which authorizes the minister to enter into a contract without Treasury Board authority in any amount at all, provided that in his opinion the contract must be entered into immediately in the interests of defence. This was perhaps a wise provision at one time, but it does seem that perhaps it gives the minister unlimited authority which is not required. This particular authority is being removed by means of the amendment to the act which is now before the house.

When deciding which procurement should be undertaken locally and which should be undertaken on a national basis we apply the principle that we should follow the procedure which will obtain the best value for the taxpayer's dollar. One has to offset administrative expense in regard to the calling of national tenders for relatively small orders, to satisfy purely local demands, against the slightly higher cost. He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the house very long over this bill; I am sure it can be passed very quickly. This bill is only common sense, as I will try to point out, and it will be well understood why there has been great need for it for some time.
In September 1964 a Dutch couple were refused Canadian citizenship because they would not take an oath stating "so help me God". To this wording there is no alternative, even within the Bill of Rights. According to the Bill of Rights freedom of religion does not allow freedom of no religion. Second, the Bill

The main purpose of this bill is to declare the rights of Canadians and those who want to become Canadians to freedom of conscience in pledging allegiance by providing that any person in Canada may affirm his allegiance as well as swear to it. A second purpose is to enlarge the pledge specifically to include Canada as well as sovereign. A third purpose is to validate oaths that have been taken in the past, as well as those that may be taken in the future, by persons without religious belief. A fourth purpose is to validate affirmations of allegiance that may have been administered in the past where, by law, an oath of allegiance should have been administered. And finally, this bill would bring the Oaths of Allegiance Act into conformity with the Royal Style and Titles Act, 1952-53 acts, Chapter 9.

Hord of the United Church, who said, at the time this subject received much publicity in the press:
Canadians boast of their freedom. We are not free to believe in God if we are not free to disbelieve.

Because the law of Canada, as interpreted by district and provincial courts in Ontario in the case of Mr. and Mrs. Ernest Bergsma, seem to bar from Canadian citizenship persons who do not believe in God and are thereby unable to take the required oath, and
Because Baptists have traditionally opposed any religious test as prerequisite to the enjoyment of civil liberties-either political or economic, and Because this law deprives a prospective citizen of liberties enjoyed by native Canadians,
WE-although we believe that faith in God is essential to a full and complete life-
Therefore
(a)	commend Mr. and Mrs. Bergsma for their honesty in refusing to invoke the name of a deity in which they do not believe,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak to Bill C-24, which is to amend the Oaths of Allegiance Act. The question before us raises further interesting questions, some of them legal, some religious. While I have little familiarity with the legal aspects of Canadian life I do claim to have some familiarity with the religious aspects.
The very question which is considered in this bill, the question of an oath, is somewhat anachronistic, since the roots of this question are buried in the past of our society and in the past of other societies which are much older than ours.
In the past, swearing an oath was taken very seriously. When you gave a man your blessing, and this was taken very seriously, the recipient of the blessing knew that you intended only good things, only pleasant things to happen to him. On the other hand, when a man was cursed, everyone knew that
February 9, 1968

the curse was intended to inflict an undoubted tragedy on the recipient in the unforeseen future. Men took seriously what they said on their honour and what they said under oath.
These days we do not believe nearly so much that the taking of an oath involves the forging of a bond, in some supernatural manner, with a supernatural being. In earlier days people believed something like that. In days gone by people believed in a very real sense that when they swore an oath the divinity was involved. The idea that the divinity is involved is retained in our modem concepts of oath taking, though to a somewhat lesser extent. For instance, in the past when a man swore to uphold his rights as a citizen he was, in a very real sense, expressing his veneration and affiliation with the divinity.
In earlier societies a man's right to citizenship was related to his religious beliefs and development. If a man had reached that stage in life where he felt that he should be accepted as a citizen of a country, he was quite willing to express his belief in and affirm his respect for God.
As the first speaker and introducer of the bill said, our society has moved away from its earlier concepts. Today we believe that for a man to have freedom of religion he must also be free to have no religion. He must be able to say that he does not believe in God. It has been said by many theologians that if man has free will, he has the concomitant freedom to deny the existence of God. As a result the question before us this afternoon entails an accurate reflection of our present society and also a refinement of theological understanding.
Though in an earlier age a man knew what you were talking about when you talked of God, today, when a group of people get together and discuss God, it is difficult for us to know what they mean. Not only in Christianity but in many other religions there is discussion, controversy and confusion, not so much about whether, as one theologian said, "God is," but as to what form He takes. The question becomes very complex and in our search for God we tend to distinguish between God and the state.
This afternoon I wish to talk about the clearcut distinction between man's religious rights and convictions and his allegiance to the state. We have opted for a society which understands the value of an independent church, a church that can reflect on and be the conscience of man and the state. I think it is a mark of maturity in our society that we can distinguish between a man's religious
Oaths of Allegiance Act convictions and his convictions as a citizen. As our Lord himself said in an earlier age, we must render unto God that which is God's and unto Caesar those things which are Caesar's. To the detriment of our society do we lump God and the state together.
Having taken this short diversion into theology I wish to return to the substance of the bill that is before us. It raises some interesting questions about the quality of citizenship in our country today. For instance, we all know that when a person decides to come to this country, decides to become a resident of Canada and a citizen of Canada, he must meet a considerable number of conditions. There is a waiting period of about five years; often this is considered a period of probation during which he must show certain minimum qualities in order to be acceptable as a Canadian. He must study diligently the history of our country and the social and political system under which it operates. He must write examinations and then take part in a formal ceremony of acceptance in a court. He is then officially granted citizenship. In other words, he is acceptable as a Canadian citizen.
I suggest that few in this chamber have undergone that experience, and this is unfortunate. A person said to me the other night that in this country there are two great roles, two great professions, for which one needs absolutely no qualifications. Both professions or functions go to the very heart and soul of our nation. Both need absolutely no qualification. One is to be an elected member of parliament, legislature or city council; the other is to become a parent.
I have had some experience with the political aspect and I am on the threshold of the other.

Yet I thinir the person who made the observation about our society should have included a third factor, and that is that most Canadians inherit their citizenship. They are Canadians, not because they have chosen to be, not because they have had a chance to exercise a choice, but through accident. They are accidental Canadians. They were born into this country, as I was, and they have inherited their citizenship. They have not had to undergo any trial period. There was no probation, no examination for formal acceptance, and most personally distressing to some of us is the fact that

Oaths of Allegiance Act we have no real way of proving we have citizenship. We have no certificates to hand up indicating that we are citizens of this country. I suppose such certificates can be obtained from the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) for $2 each, and I doubt if there are any extensive examinations, apart from the financial penalty, that would prevent any of us from obtaining them.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Earlier this year we had some discussion in this house about reducing the voting age to 18. There is also something very easy about inheriting the right to vote in Canada. I suggest that we should make much more of our inheriting of Canadian citizenship, not perhaps in a legal way because it might smack of so many other things that are against the grain of tradition. Instead of allowing only our new Canadians to have all the benefit of education for citizenship and for the ceremony that I am sure is invested with great meaning for them, we should assist our accidental Canadians, and these comprise the majority of us, to a more useful development in citizenship through a co-ordination of activities in our schools and other community ventures. If the right to vote has any meaning it has to be tied to the meaning of citizenship itself.
I congratulate the hon. member who introduced this bill in an attempt to clean up one of the anachronisms that exist under our current citizenship laws, but I would suggest we go further to make citizenship meaningful for all Canadians, both those who are new and those who are accidental.

I think there are very few of us in this house who will forget the Bergsma case when it occurred in 1965, and when the hon. member who introduced this bill gave it so much attention, attention which it rightly deserved.
I am interested in the hon. member's bill because a somewhat similar case occurred in my riding of Victoria, B.C. It concerned a family by the name of van der Pol who, under similar circumstances, were denied the right of citizenship because the judge of the citizenship court when hearing their application, and understanding they refused to give the oath of allegiance, returned the certificates to Ottawa and refused them citizenship.
I hope that this important private members bill before us today will come to a vote. To try

and establish just exactly what I will be voting for if it does, I have gone into the bill as carefully as I could. I have sought the advice of experts, because I am not a lawyer, to interpret some of the implications of the bill. I found this difficult to do, and it points up one of the frustrations of being a private member of this house, in that we have so much to do, so little time to do it in, and so few facilities to help us. Because of this I have found great difficulty in marshalling my thoughts on the matter, but I hope this will not be too obvious to hon. members as I try to outline them. How much easier it would be for all of us if, as private members, we had more research assistance; how much more intelligently we could vote on bills presented to us, such as this bill, if we were able to devote more time to research or had more facilities available to us. I know that this is in the works and that sooner or later we will get more assistance. I most certainly look forward to that day, and I know that a lot of other members do so, as well.
Returning now to Bill C-24 which has to do with the oath of allegiance, may I say that laws are made for the public. They apply to laymen and they must be understood by laymen. As I understand it, as a layman, when one becomes a citizen the taking on of citizenship also assumes the taking on of responsibility for obedience to law, and the taking on of responsibility in the defence of one's country. To give solemn significance to the taking on of such responsibility the oath of allegiance is taken on the Bible, and at the end of it we use the solemn words, "so help me God." The reason for this has been outlined by the previous speaker.
To digress in a personal vein for a moment, Mr. Speaker, and speaking of defending one's country, it has always seemed rather curious to me that the first time the oath of allegiance appears in Canadian law is in the British North America Act, an act of the British House of Commons. I cannot speak for either of the other services but I do know that in the British navy they do not swear an oath of allegiance. Members of the Royal Navy, defenders of the crown and defenders of the country, are not required to be sworn men. In the British navy no officers and no men take an oath of allegiance. Neither did we in the Royal Canadian Navy, as I recall it, until some time during the war when certain members were required to take the oath of allegiance. Those responsible, however, seemed to overlook some of the other men, including

myself, and in fact they did not catch up with me until some time around 1952. In the Royal Navy the only exception to this rule was the Royal Marines, who were sworn men.
The substitute for the taking of an oath of allegiance in the British navy was that, every quarter, all members of every ship and establishment were mustered and the Articles of War, which state what a man's conduct is to be in the line of duty, in the face of the enemy and so forth, are read by the commanding officer to the men lined up and, to signify the difference between sworn men and those not sworn, the sworn men were allowed to leave their caps on. These, as I say, were the Royal Marines.
When we in the Canadian navy were required to swear the oath of allegiance we continued with the quarterly reading of the Articles of War, but we still carried on with the matter of taking off our caps, regardless of whether we were sworn or not. I bring this up to show that sometimes traditions are carried on after they have ceased to have any meaning.
Returning to the bill under discussion, Mr. Speaker, I notice that in my research I uncovered the same references which the sponsor of the bill uncovered. At the time of the Bergsma case the public press came out very strongly in support of the suggestion that the law should be changed to permit people to take the oath of allegiance without swearing an oath, not that this was supporting the fact that they should not have any religious convictions but supporting the stand that freedom to believe presupposes freedom to disbelieve.

I accept that. Mr. Speaker, the Oaths of Allegiance Act as it stands at present supplies a form of oath of allegiance for use whenever any person is required by law, or desires, to take an oath of allegiance. There are only two stated exceptions-the oath required under the British North America Act, 1867, and the one required by the Canadian Citizenship Act. In both cases the form of oath to be used, which has already been read in the house by previous speakers, is set out.
The act also provides in section 3 that in certain cases no other oath is required, and provides in section 4 for the time within which the oath may be taken. Section 5 of the act allows the prescribed oath to be affirmed by "all persons allowed by law in civil cases in any part of Canada to affirm instead of making oaths". The last section of the act, section 6, designates what persons may administer the oath as set out in the act.
We have perhaps heard enough about the Bergsma case, so I shall not go into that, although I have some fairly extensive notes which I made in respect of that case. In view of the judgment of the court of appeal of Ontario in the Bergsma case I wonder whether any change in the existing law is required in order to achieve the main purpose of the hon. member's bill as set out in the explanatory notes. I have already explained how it seemed to apply to the courts in British Columbia.
The bill would eliminate the two stated exceptions-the British North America Act

February 9, 1968
Oaths of Allegiance Act and the Citizenship Act-retaining only that portion of the British North America Act provision which relates to the provinces, which a federal act could not change in any event. The result would be that the oath of allegiance set out in the amended act would purport to apply to the Canadian Citizenship Act and the British North America Act. Having spoken to members of the legal profession I am of the opinion that it is doubtful whether this would be the actual result, because the bill does not purport to repeal the oath of allegiance set out in the Canadian Citizenship Act, or any of those sections of the Canadian Citizenship Act that specifically state that the oath of allegiance required to gain citizenship is the oath set out in the Citizenship Act. In view of the judgment in the Bergsma case it would appear undesirable to confuse the situation by any amendment at all, but if an amendment still was thought to be desirable the better method of proceeding would be simply to amend the Citizenship Act itself.
I might make an incidental comment concerning the form of the oath. The draft bill is said to enlarge the oath in the existing act by adding the requirement of observing the laws of Canada and fulfilling one's duties as a Canadian citizen. These things may have some relevance to a person newly acquiring citizenship under the Citizenship Act, as being a promise for the future that he must make as a condition under a grant of citizenship, but as noted at the outset the Oaths of Allegiance Act does not purport to provide an oath for that purpose. It provides an oath for other general occasions where it might be required or desirable to have someone swear an oath of allegiance. This was presumably to include persons who already are Canadian citizens and who already have been obeying the laws of Canada and fulfilling their duties as Canadian citizens.
While it probably does no harm to draw these matters to the attention of a person who is already a Canadian citizen, nevertheless it hardly seems appropriate that these matters should be added to a general oath of allegiance. Furthermore, on grounds of policy one may question the two objects of validating past oaths that were wrongly given to persons who, at law, were unable to swear, and of validating past affirmations that should have been oaths. Rewriting the past is, even if justified, somewhat unusual; but unless we are dealing with specific and known instances of injustice, little can be said in favour of a retrospective amendment. At any rate it is

not clear that the purpose is accomplished by the wording in the draft bill. The bill in its proposed amendment to section 5 of the act, in the first subsection, reads as follows:
Where, prior to the 1st day of January 1967 or thereafter, an oath has been duly administered and taken, the fact that the person to whom the oath was administered had, at the time of taking the oath, no religious belief, shall not for any purpose affect the validity of such oath.
Presumably the reference to "an oath" would be broad enough to refer to any oath, not just an oath of allegiance, and the implication that the words "of allegiance" would be read into the section may be open to some doubt because they are included specifically in the second subsection of the proposed section 5 which reads as follows:
5.(2) Where, prior to the 1st day of January, 1967, an affirmation of allegiance has been made instead of an oath of allegiance taken, that fact shall not for any purpose affect the validity of such affirmation which shall be of the same force and effect as if the person who made his affirmation had taken the oath.
Moreover, in conclusion it seems to me that if on its face the proposed new subsection applies to all oaths, it might be declared ultra vires. Therefore I feel that while I sympathize with the objective of this bill I cannot vote for it.

They felt that the word of a good man was always good and one did not have to buttress it in this way.
Many countries, as we know, in our own western tradition do not require swearing of

the oath. The constitution of the United States indicates that the president may assume office and take the oath either by swearing or by affirmation. Interestingly enough, I understand that not a single president has even chosen to affirm. They all have been prepared to swear. It is not surprising, of course, that this should be the case in a country like the United States which, in its inception, laid great stress on the separation of the church and state. This was very much a part of the thinking of the philosophers and political figures of the eighteenth century.
The separation of the church and the state is something very appealing. Many of us are attracted and impressed by the thought that secular institutions like schools should not be schools for religious instruction. Many believe that we should separate the church from the state, and that the state should allow the church to function freely within it. This appeals to many.
On the other hand, there are few things which are clear-cut, or black or white. Our own state is not a wholly secular state. Many of our institutional patterns of government and society are based upon Judaic law and Christian precept. We always open our sittings here with the ceremony of prayers, to which the public are not invited, for historic reasons which I shan't go into.
This bill does to my mind have much merit. It provides for those people who are not Christians; it provides for those people who are not believers in any God or gods, and another group of people, I think not mentioned so far-those Christians inclined to believe that man should not swear. They take very literally the injunction against swearing "by anything in heaven because it is the Lords, or by anything on earth because it is his footstool." These people believe that man should not swear.
Another thing that is very disturbing about the compulsion to oath taking is that it instils hypocrisy. You must take an oath. You have no belief in any deity but you comply and you invoke a deity. This leads to and spreads hypocrisy. As that great debunker of an earlier day, George Bernard Shaw, said: "Sir, I am an atheist, and I thank God for it." This is the sort of situation we are developing by the existing legislation.
